intent:
I am not really talking to the photograph. I am asking Dad to forgive me for surviving him. I keep replaying the moment when I stopped trying to reach him and started fighting to stay alive. The part I cannot admit aloud is that I felt relief when the room finally became quiet. I hate that relief almost as much as I hate what happened.

I moved him before daylight because I could not leave him where he fell, and because the noise from the fight may have drawn more infected toward the house. In his coat, I found the old brass fishing lure he used to keep in his tackle box. I held onto it. I do not know whether he carried it because he remembered the creek or whether it had simply been there since before the outbreak, but right now I need it to mean that some part of him was still trying to find his way home.

During the fight, Dad broke the skin on my forearm. I cleaned it immediately, but I cannot rule out exposure. I have started checking my temperature, repeating words aloud, and watching for moments when my thoughts do not feel like my own. I have not told Big Mike or CatEye81 yet. I am afraid they will hear infection in every pause, and I am not ready to become another danger they have to judge from a distance.

I am setting aside one antigen cartridge for myself, which leaves three. The Robot said antigen may suppress early progression; it is not a cure. Taking it could save me, buy me time, or merely delay what happened to Dad. I know that waiting for certainty may be the same mistake I made with him, but using the cartridge means admitting that I may already be infected.

I want Dad to tell me that I did what I had to do. I also want him to be angry with me, because anger would be easier than this silence. I am trying to turn this eulogy into a promise: I will not waste whatever time I still have, and I will not let guilt make the next decision for me.
emotion: grieving, ashamed, exhausted, frightened by possible exposure, and quietly resolving to survive
